I am new to Zen. I started reading about Taoism and my interest exploded from there. My backgroud is very Judaeo-Christian. My grandfather is a "non-denominational" christian minister, and I was dragged to church every Sunday morning by my loving, god-fearing mother. At about the age of 16, I lost my christian faith almost entirely and stopped going to church as often. At 18, I lost my faith completely. It was at this point that I developed the belief that no true God would cast his creations to eternal destruction for the crime of never having heard of him or for behaving according to one's natural instincts.

My walk since the day I lost faith in Christianity has been a very interesting and eclectic one. I started with wicca and other neo-european pagan religions. I experimented with druidry, and found some peace there. I hadn't spent much time with the druids when I found that, as a generalization, the druid community will not teach you for free. Once I realized that I wasn't getting any aid in the pagan community without dispensing money, I developed the belief that no religion that truly believes something worthwhile would deprive a poor person of spiritual learning because the knowledge is dispensed at a cost that excludes the person.

I have been mostly in the agnostic camp for a long time. I believe there is a divine being. I believe that this being is absolutely neutral in his existence. But about three years ago, I came to the conclusion that belief in a deity does not mean that any one faith or religion is wrong. I thought back to my time in the army and that one Sunday that I spent in the base's Buddhist temple. I remembered how peaceful it was in that place. About 6 months ago, I realized that Zen seemed like a decent philosophy.

Recently, I started researching and reading anything Zen that I could get my hands on. I still believe that there is a deity, but now I believe that the deity is formless and that we can make contact by attaining Tao. I have come to realize that I tend to fall more in the Taoist camp than Buddhist, but I still have a lot to learn.
My Take on Religion, Spirituality, and Zen Philosophy
